title: Ezekiel 21:1–17
context: The LORD tells Ezekiel to set his face toward Jerusalem and prophesy against the sanctuaries and the land of Israel: the LORD will draw his sword from its sheath and cut off both righteous and wicked, so that all flesh will know he has drawn it. This explains the fire in the forest of 20:45–49. The LORD tells Ezekiel to sigh with a broken heart before the people and, when asked, to say that news is coming that will make every heart melt. A second word follows, the song of the sword, sharpened and polished for slaughter and handed to the killer; Ezekiel is told to cry and wail, beat his thigh, and strike his hands together, and the LORD says he too will strike his hands and cause his wrath to rest. Several lines, especially in verses 10 and 13 about the rod, are difficult in Hebrew and are translated in different ways. The cutting off of righteous and wicked alike describes the sweep of a national disaster and is commonly read alongside 9:4 and 18:20, where God distinguishes the righteous. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage soberly as a prophetic lament over coming judgment on Jerusalem. The Hebrew numbering of this chapter is noted at 20:45–49.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Ezekiel. The parable of the forest in the south is about to be explained.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the continuation of the previous message. Both traditions commonly read the verse as introducing the interpretation of the fire in the south.

verses.text: “Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and preach toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to set his face toward Jerusalem and prophesy against the sanctuaries and the land. The south is now named.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the parable of 20:46 explained: the forest is Jerusalem and the land of Israel. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as clarifying the target of judgment.

verses.text: Tell the land of Israel, ‘The LORD says: “Behold, I am against you, and will draw my sword out of its sheath, and will cut off from you the righteous and the wicked.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD drawing his sword to cut off righteous and wicked alike. The disaster will sweep across the nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the comprehensive reach of a national judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse alongside 9:4 and 18:20, where God distinguishes the righteous.

verses.text: Seeing then that I will cut off from you the righteous and the wicked, therefore my sword will go out of its sheath against all flesh from the south to the north.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sword going out against all flesh from south to north. No region of the land will escape its reach.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the universal scope of the coming calamity. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as a description of national catastrophe.

verses.text: All flesh will know that I, the LORD, have drawn my sword out of its sheath. It will not return any more.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see that all flesh will know the LORD has drawn his sword, which will not return. The judgment is decisive.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s purpose in judgment openly revealed. Both traditions commonly read the verse as underscoring the certainty of what is coming.

verses.text: “Therefore sigh, you son of man. You shall sigh before their eyes with a broken heart and with bitterness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to sigh with a broken heart before the people. The prophet feels the weight of the message.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet embodying grief over judgment (compare Jeremiah 4:19). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that God’s messenger is not indifferent.

verses.text: It shall be, when they ask you, ‘Why do you sigh?’ that you shall say, ‘Because of the news, for it comes! Every heart will melt, all hands will be feeble, every spirit will faint, and all knees will be weak as water. Behold, it comes, and it shall be done, says the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel explaining that news is coming that will make every heart melt and every knee weak. Fear will be universal.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the certainty of the coming judgment, it shall be done. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober warning delivered with compassion.

verses.text: The LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD’s word coming to Ezekiel again. A new oracle about the sword begins, sharper than the first.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see another word from God introducing the song of the sword. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as marking a new section.

verses.text: “Son of man, prophesy, and say, ‘The LORD says: “A sword! A sword! It is sharpened, and also polished.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the cry, A sword! A sword! sharpened and polished. The image is vivid and urgent, meant to wake the hearers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sword as an image of God’s judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as poetic language for coming war.

verses.text: It is sharpened that it may make a slaughter. It is polished that it may be as lightning. Should we then make mirth? The rod of my son condemns every tree.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sword sharpened for slaughter and polished like lightning. Celebration is out of place when judgment is near.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the warning against mirth in the face of judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as a call to take God’s judgment seriously.

verses.text: It is given to be polished, that it may be handled. The sword is sharpened. Yes, it is polished to give it into the hand of the killer.” ’
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sword polished to be handed to the killer. God’s judgment works through human agents and their weapons.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God directing the instrument of judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse soberly, as poetic language for the coming Babylonian assault.

verses.text: Cry and wail, son of man; for it is on my people. It is on all the princes of Israel. They are delivered over to the sword with my people. Therefore beat your thigh.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD telling Ezekiel to cry, wail, and beat his thigh because the sword is on his people and princes. Grief is fitting.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s lament as a sign of the severity of judgment. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a call to mourn rather than gloat.

verses.text: “For there is a trial. What if even the rod that condemns will be no more?” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a trial announced and a question about the rod that condemns. The people are being tested by what is coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God testing his people through judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse within the song of the sword, holding its details with care.

verses.text: “You therefore, son of man, prophesy, and strike your hands together. Let the sword be doubled the third time, the sword of the fatally wounded. It is the sword of the great one who is fatally wounded, which enters into their rooms.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Ezekiel told to prophesy and strike his hands together as the sword is doubled. The sign-act emphasizes the intensity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the prophet’s gesture as a sign of the coming judgment (compare 6:11). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse soberly.

verses.text: I have set the threatening sword against all their gates, that their heart may melt, and their stumblings be multiplied. Ah! It is made as lightning. It is pointed for slaughter.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the threatening sword set against all the gates so hearts melt and stumbling increases. The city’s defenses fail.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s judgment reaching every entrance of the city. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober picture of a city under siege.

verses.text: Gather yourselves together. Go to the right. Set yourselves in array. Go to the left, wherever your face is set.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sword commanded to go right and left wherever it is directed. Its movement is purposeful, not random.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the sword as an instrument under God’s direction. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as poetic language for judgment.

verses.text: I will also strike my hands together, and I will cause my wrath to rest. I, the LORD, have spoken it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD striking his hands together and causing his wrath to rest. The judgment will reach its end.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God declaring his word fulfilled, I, the LORD, have spoken it. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the solemn close of the song of the sword.
